newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Emerging markets regain lustre for money managers.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets regain lustre for money managers.

text.p: The world's money managers, at a "crystal ball" session on the shores of Lake Geneva, predicted on Tuesday that emerging markets will outshine developed cousins in 1997 on Western cash inflows, local liquidity and growth.
Fund managers at an international investment conference expected a reallocation of assets away from the rich world in 1997 to produce a healthy flow of funds into emerging markets.

"With very strong earnings in emerging markets, I expect them to outperform, not just catch up with the developed world," said Arnab Banerji, chief investment officer at London's Foreign & Colonial Emerging Markets with $5 billion under management.
"There will be a rotation out of developed markets and a reallocation of assets away from the U.S. into emerging markets," he told the conference.

"Expectations of investors in emerging markets are rock-bottom. We've had three years of under-performance and I believe that's coming to an end. Rising domestic and international liquidity will be the icing on the cake."
Despite rallies in Eastern Europe and Russia and in smaller liquidity-driven markets like Venezuela and Bangladesh, emerging markets in 1996 failed to provide the dizzying returns of 1993.
But cash flows into the developing world should continue to recover in 1997, lured by prospects of lower interest rates, high domestic liquidity and high growth, money managers said.

Michael Howell, head of London's Crossborder Capital and a respected emerging market economist, said $50 billion of the world's money flew into emerging markets in 1996 -- up from $15 billion in 1995, $40 billion in 1994 and compared to 1993's peak of $63 billion.
"In 1997, we expect flows to be similar to this year's $50 billion," he added.
In 1997, Howell predicted that South European markets would outshine East Europe where he saw signs of start of overheating.
In Asia, he saw value at "bargain levels" in South Korea -- "at its cheapest in 30 years" -- and Chile as well as good value in India, Indonesia and the Philippines.

Banerji said his favourite picks for 1997 were Brazil, India, Egypt and Chile which he said would deliver a 25-45 percent return in the next 12 months. "They're cheap and domestic liquidity is rising," he said.
He was particularly keen on Poland -- "If you wanted to go away for 15 years and wanted a place to put your money, it would be Poland. That's our favourite."

In the regional race to lure money managers, Asian emerging markets enjoyed the biggest inflow of global funds in 1996 with $2.56 billion, followed by Latin America with 1.53 billion and East Europe and Africa with 1.08 billion, a survey of mutual fund asset allocations showed.

The survey by Micropal, a London-based market analysis company which tracks 38,000 mutual funds in the $6.5 trillion global fund industry, also said Mexico was the most favourite destination for global emerging market equity funds this year, followed by South Korea, India, South Africa and Brazil.

Global equity market fund managers poured a net $758 million into Mexico in the past 12 months, followed by $752 million with South Korea, $708 million with India, $584 million with South Africa and $570 million with Brazil.

Regional fund managers in Asia put more faith into China and Hong Kong than their global counterparts. Global fund managers placed only $152 million in China and Hong Kong in the past 12 months compared to $914 million by Asian regional funds.
